meaning: Military force associated with Judah and Benjamin—the fighting strength and loyalty of the tribes toward the house of David
description: The number 180,000 appears three times in the Bible, and each time in a military context. In 1 Kings 12:21 and the parallel verse 2 Chronicles 11:1, Rehoboam gathers 180,000 chosen warriors from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin to fight against the northern tribes after the kingdom was divided. In 2 Chronicles 17:18, 180,000 men equipped for battle under Josabad are mentioned in King Jehoshaphat's army. The number is thus consistently linked to the military capacity of those tribes that remained loyal to the house of David. Although 180,000 does not have an independent symbolic tradition in classical Jewish literature, its repeated use underscores the fighting strength of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin and their loyalty to the promised royal dynasty.

versions.meaning: The number 180,000 has no well-established independent symbolic meaning in biblical or Jewish tradition.
versions.description: The number 180,000 does not appear as a central symbolic number in the Bible or in classical Jewish literature. It can be broken down into factors such as 18 (chai, meaning 'life' in Hebrew) and 10,000 (which may symbolize a vast multitude or completeness), but the combination itself carries no recognized symbolism. Large numbers in the Bible are often used to express military strength or census figures, yet 180,000 as an independent symbol is not prominent in tradition.

versions.meaning: Number of selected warriors from Judah and Benjamin—military strength and tribal loyalty
versions.description: The number 180,000 appears three times in the Bible, and each time in a military context. In 1 Kings 12:21 and the parallel verse 2 Chronicles 11:1, Rehoboam gathers 180,000 chosen warriors from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin to fight against the northern tribes after the kingdom was divided. In 2 Chronicles 17:18, 180,000 men equipped for battle under Josabad are mentioned in King Jehoshaphat's army. The number is thus consistently linked to the military capacity of those tribes that remained loyal to the house of David. Although 180,000 does not have an independent symbolic tradition in classical Jewish literature, its repeated use underscores the fighting strength of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin and their loyalty to the promised royal dynasty.

footnotes.text: The number 180,000 can be decomposed as 18 × 10,000. In Hebrew, the number 18 has a gematria value corresponding to the word חי (chai, 'life'), while 10,000 (revava) often symbolizes an overwhelming multitude in biblical language. However, this decomposition holds no established place in classical Jewish numerology.

Rehoboam's attempt to gather 180,000 warriors against Israel was halted by the prophet Shemaiah, who delivered God's word that the tribes should not fight each other (1 Kings 12:22–24). The army was never deployed, showing that the large number serves as a contrast to God's sovereign intervention.

The fact that parallel accounts in the Books of Kings and Chronicles give the same figure (180,000) suggests a fixed tradition linked to this number. The Chronicler also repeats the number in connection with Jehoshaphat's army, which may reflect a literary convention for denoting Judah's total military capacity.

The current formulation focuses primarily on the Rehoboam event, while 2 Chr 17:18 concerns the strength of Jehoshaphat's army forces.
